newsitem.title: UK: Rural army marches to defend UK country sports.
newsitem.headline: Rural army marches to defend UK country sports.

text.p: A rural army gathered from the length and breadth of Britain is marching on London on Thursday to defend traditional countryside sports from the threat of extinction.

Gamekeepers, farmers, farriers and hunters are walking to the capital from as far afield as the Lake District in the north and Cornwall in the south-west in support of a way of life seen as under attack from a new Labour government more at home with football than fishing.
Spurred by proposed legislation to ban fox hunting, some 100,000 people are expected to converge on London's Hyde Park for a rally.

Buses, trains and planes from Ireland, France and Northern Ireland are bringing protesters to the capital for a show of strength which organisers hope will match the 1930s Jarrow march against unemployment.
"If needs be I am prepared to go to prison for defending our countryside and our heritage," said Arnold Harvey, editor of Horse and Hound magazine.

The Countryside Marches and Rally, a coalition of sportsmen and women plus people employed in the countryside, say that rural pursuits provide employment for some 90,000 people and attract more than four million participants.
The target of their wrath is a parliamentary bill by Labour MP Michael Foster, due to be debated in November, which would ban the hunting of foxes, deer, hares and mink with dogs.
Foster denounces hunting as a "cruel and barbaric practice which should have ended centuries ago along with cock-fighting, bear-baiting and dog-fighting."

With the newly-elected Labour government commanding a thumping 179 seat parliamentary majority, Foster's bill is probably the gravest threat that fox hunting has ever faced and has raised fears that fishing would be next in line for the axe.

Dressed in yellow T-shirts bearing slogans such as "Give Country Jobs a Sporting Chance", the men and women who have spent three weeks on the road want to demonstrate that hunting is not merely a jolly sport for a few privileged landowners.
"If hunting were to disappear the face of the countryside will change forever," said Sam Butler, secretary of the Warwickshire hunt.

"If those who stand to lose their livelihoods are forced to move to the towns, village schools and shops will close down and the vacuum will be filled by those who can afford to live in the countryside and commute to work in towns and cities," Butler said.
The marchers have encountered nothing but encouragement on their walk to London, where they will hear speeches from supporters such as former Conservative deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine.

Britain's strong animal rights lobby has so far watched silently from the sidelines and several groups who regularly indulge in hunt sabotage have urged their supporters to stay away from Thursday's rally.

They are making their views known through a 1.5 million signature petition protesting at the killing of animals for entertainment which is being presented to Prime Minister Tony Blair's official Downing Street residence on Thursday.
"We anticipate that the number of people who have signed this petition will outnumber those attending the rally by at least 50 to one," said Neil Hansen, one of the organisers of the petition.
